## User-confirmed corrections and scope (12 October 2026)

These answers supersede conflicting résumé wording. Source: user's second message.

- Use Ada Mensah and Mosslink publicly. Exclude employer and employment dates from site and downloadable CV; current employment details not confirmed. Do not imply a formal current title.
- Ada wrote firmware, scheduled power states and built the bring-up fixture. Colleague designed PCB and analogue front end. Do not claim Ada owned complete sensor or hardware design.
- Two-year figure is a projection from bench currents and an assumed reporting cycle; longest run 72 hours. No field endurance or weather testing supports two-year claim. Reporting interval and calculation attribution remain unconfirmed; omit them.
- Forty engineering samples assembled, six tested on bench, none to customers. No field pilot or product launch. Do not claim Ada personally assembled/tested all units.
- One preliminary emissions check passed; full qualification unfinished. Never certified or qualified.
- Radio-awake problem was seen in a current trace after failed transmission. Cause, fix, timing and later resolution unconfirmed; all excluded. No trace available.
- Own fixture photograph and simplified power-state diagram have public-use permission. Photograph remains unavailable. Colleague circuit diagram has no permission and is excluded.
- Supplied SVGs may stand in as labelled explanations only. Neither is photograph, original wiring, firmware, current trace or test result. Sleep/Measure/Transmit is a teaching sequence with no durations/current values.
- Audience: firmware hiring manager. Purpose: understand how Ada connects code to measurable signal.
- Working documents: state table, timing diagram, current trace. Bring-up means checking new board's basic operation. Prior notes also establish bench checklists.
- Lesson in user's words: a firmware decision needs a physical observation; estimate and observed run support different claims. No implication every issue resolved or every device tested.
- Public example email: ada@example.com, link only. Do not send email or claim tested delivery.
- Make corrected printable HTML CV downloadable; no invented PDF. No old site or testimonials.
- Mosslink only project; include dedicated project page and main-story appearance. No invented project, photograph, testimonial, award or result.
- English; ordinary navigation; share preview; site icon; useful missing-page page. No blog/chat/translation/form. Legal/jurisdiction deferred to publishing; no compliance claim.
- Local system fonts, supplied local drawings or original explanatory geometry only. No external purchase/download. No additional skills installed; user declined.
- Unconfirmed facts stay out. Employer/dates and unavailable artifacts are excluded, not blockers.

## Remaining unanswered facts

- Reporting interval, model author, cause/fix/resolution of radio issue, exact individual test/assembly scope and current formal employment details. None may be inferred or used.
- Public use of employer-specific hardware detail is not established: use generic explanatory geometry, never a reconstruction.
# Three concepts — awaiting user choice

Premise: Ada wrote firmware, scheduled power states and built the Mosslink bring-up fixture. Her lesson connects decisions to physical observations and distinguishes projections from observed runs. No concept assumes a radio cause/fix, field deployment or completed qualification.

Trade forms considered: state table, timing diagram, bench checklist, bring-up procedure, measurement log, qualification checklist. The first three are grounded in Ada's working documents/notes. Local geometry is original explanation, never a reconstruction or measured evidence.

## A. At the fixture (recommended)

- Question: How do you connect a firmware decision to a physical observation?
- Form: bench checklist. Chapters: Purpose (opening/name), Firmware scope (who), Bring-up (how), Power states (Mosslink work), Observation (radio-awake problem), Evidence limits (outcomes with qualifications), Handover (answer/contact).
- Object: seven chunky socket/contact modules forming a generic bring-up fixture with brass pins. Not actual PCB or wiring.
- Transformations: opening modules join as fixture; bring-up opens into command-to-observation path; evidence separates model/run groups; ending reconnects fixture.
- Opening draws from Ada's stated lesson and fixture authorship, not an invented origin anecdote. Close: a decision needs observation, and evidence limits remain explicit; email/CV/project links.
- Stands on confirmed firmware, fixture, daily documents, radio observation and corrected model/run/sample/qualification facts.
- Needs no additional asset/permission. Supplied bring-up teaching SVG may explain the relationship, clearly labelled.
- Why theirs: Ada built the fixture and wants hiring managers to see the connection between her firmware and bench observations.
- Runnable sketch: /sketch/fixture (Purpose, Observation, Handover).

## B. Power-state selector

- Question: What can a power-state schedule tell us—and what must we observe?
- Form: state table. Chapters: Scope (opening), Responsibilities (who), States (how), Transition (radio observation), Evidence (projection/run distinction), Next action (lesson/contact).
- Object: seven solid radial switch modules form an original teaching selector. It is not a device Ada built.
- Transformations: opening circular selector; states become an opened teaching sequence; evidence groups distinguish estimate and observed run; close selector returns whole.
- Opening asks schedule question; close states that model and physical observation have different evidential roles.
- Stands on Ada's power scheduling, use of state tables, confirmed radio observation and estimate/run lesson. No recovered firmware state sequence claimed.
- Needs nothing additional; supplied Sleep/Measure/Transmit diagram can be a teaching explanation only.
- Why theirs: makes the limits of Mosslink's projected endurance central to her power scheduling story.
- Runnable sketch: /sketch/states (Scope, Transition, Next action).

## C. Observation lead

- Question: Where does a firmware claim meet its evidence?
- Form: timing-diagram reading. Chapters: Signal question (opening), Firmware decision (who/how), State sequence (illustrative), Bench observation (radio issue), Observation window (projection versus run), Reading (answer/contact).
- Object: seven thick cylindrical sleeves form a generic bench observation lead. Metaphorical, not actual equipment/wiring.
- Transformations: opening connected lead; middle separates command and observation along reading axis; evidence divides model/run portions without plotted values; ending reconnects lead.
- Opening connects claim to physical observation. Close states the evidence window rather than an invented debugging resolution.
- Stands on timing diagrams/current traces as working documents, firmware ownership, 72-hour run and user lesson.
- Needs no additional asset. No actual trace available; no synthetic trace presented as evidence.
- Why theirs: the distinction between Mosslink's observed run and projected life determines how the lead opens and what the ending says.
- Runnable sketch: /sketch/lead (Signal question, Observation window, Reading).

## Assessment and scope

All three use one continuing tangible object, meaningful transformations and complete HTML with name, firmware work, contact and evidence limits. A best passes the personal-object test because it is drawn from something Ada actually built. B and C are explicitly teaching metaphors and weaker on personal specificity. Shared sketch colors are provisional, not the later look decision.

Final site also needs ordinary navigation, Mosslink project route, corrected downloadable printable HTML CV, share preview, icon and useful missing-page route. No extra projects, employer/dates, testimonials, external fonts/assets or legal-compliance claims. Publishing is user's decision.

Chosen concept: awaiting explicit selection. Next stop: full storyboard for chosen concept.
# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What it tells, in a few words | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | What its caption stands on |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **How the pieces stand:** a stack, a fan, a ring, a row, a wall, or what the chapter needs. The same pieces in every beat.
- **What is on their faces:** the person's real pictures and words. Name the picture.
- **What the chapter adds:** anything in the scene besides the pieces. Often nothing.
- **What its caption stands on:** a working title of a few words, and the lines of the fact sheet the caption will be written from. Not the caption.

**Write no captions yet.** The words are written at a later stop, where the person chooses them. A sentence written now, to make the script read well, is where a detail gets in that nobody told you: a hall that was "standing empty", a wheel that is "true again". So a beat names its facts and stops there. Where a beat wants something the fact sheet does not hold, such as what the work taught them or what was wrong before they came, put the question in its place.

For the close, state in planning notes what answers the opening question and which facts support that answer. Its final wording still waits, but its meaning must be decided. A contact link, a job goal or a promise to write an answer later does not supply that meaning.

## Someone with thirty seconds

Say how a visitor who does not scroll gets the name, what the person does, one proof of it, and how to reach them. The first screen carries the first three. A rail jumps to any chapter, and one link skips to the close.

Specify what the opening tells someone outside the field about the person's work, in ordinary words supported by the fact sheet. Explain any unfamiliar title or technical term there. This meaning is part of the plan even while the final captions wait.

## Without the scene

Say what a visitor gets in each case. The text is ordinary HTML over the scene, so all of it is there in every row. Say what stands in for the pieces.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | |
| With reduced motion | |
| With no WebGL | |
| With no JavaScript | |

## The look and the type

Both come from the object's material: plates are ceramic on linen, a status page is dark glass, a paper is white with dark ink. Name two or three looks, each as its ground, its ink, one accent, and the surface of the pieces. The person picks by scrolling, once it is built.

Two typefaces: one for the text, and one for what is printed on the pieces, which belongs to the form.

## Everything else the site needs

Mark every row build, later or never, and say who decided.

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | | |
| A page for each project | | |
| Every project listed | | |
| How to reach them, and a CV | | |
| What others say | | |
| Languages | | |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | | |
| The page for an address that is not there | | |
| A blog | | |
| A chat | | |
| A legal notice, where their country asks for one | | |

## What you ask for

A yes to the script, or what to change. Give the list of what you decided for them with it.

item.text:
I chose **At the fixture** and [recorded why](docs/story/concepts.md): you built the fixture yourself, making it more personal than the selector or lead metaphors.

The story answers: **How do you connect a firmware decision to a physical observation?**

| Chapter | Story and fixture movement |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Introduce you and your Mosslink contribution; assemble the fixture. |
| Firmware scope | Separate your firmware, scheduling and fixture work from your colleague’s hardware work. |
| Bring-up | Open the fixture into a command-to-observation path. |
| Power states | Show a clearly labelled teaching loop, without invented timings. |
| Observation | Describe the radio-awake observation without claiming a cause or fix. |
| Evidence limits | Separate projection from the 72-hour run, then explain sample testing and unfinished qualification. |
| Handover | Reconnect the fixture around your lesson; provide email and CV links. |

The [complete storyboard](docs/story/storyboard.md) also specifies ordinary navigation, the Mosslink project page, printable downloadable HTML CV, local share preview and icon, useful 404, and phone/reduced-motion/fallback behavior. It records the decisions made for you. Everything remains local.

**Does this structure work, or would you like anything changed?** Next I’ll build its opening, middle and ending in two looks for you to compare.

The [storyfolio skill](.agents/skills/storyfolio/SKILL.md) requires storyboard approval before building the chosen site: “They have said yes to it.” This checkpoint approves the story structure, not publication.
